title: Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
description: Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill tw
body: Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.Andrea Simons said a review into the "failure to monitor him appropriately" was needed after it emerged the 40-year-old was able to target his victims despite being known to police as a sexual predator.British Transport Police (BTP) said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Metropolitan Police said it had actively investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.Meanwhile, the police watchdog confirmed two officers are being investigated over their handling of Levy.The Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable was under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant was facing a misconduct investigation.The Met, BTP and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) have all admitted failures in how Levy was monitored between his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges and his arrest for murder in September 2025.On Saturday, Simons told BBC Breakfast a "multi-agency review" was needed, saying: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."Simons said public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".The Met said its detectives had "exhausted numerous lines of enquiry - including working with coroners – to identify whether Levy is responsible for any similar, unsolved incidents, including deaths".No further victims have been identified so far but the force urged "anyone who believes they may be a victim of his to contact police".Levy is known to have attacked at least 10 women on public transport in London, seeking out busy carriages to assault passengers.BTP said more women "may recognise [Levy] and have not yet reported what has happened to them".Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he committed a violent rape in January 2025.He went on to kill Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March of that year and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months later.Earlier this year he was found guilty by a jury at Inner London Crown Court of groping 10 women on the Tube and an 11th while in prison, but details of that case could only be reported this week at the conclusion of his murder trial.Those offences took place between April 2022 at the prison, followed by the Tube assaults between 24 October 2023 and May 2025.He had already been convicted of sexually assaulting two women in 2018, which he was jailed for in 2021.BTP has confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect." Lisa Squire, whose daughter Libby was murdered by a man who had previously committed a string of sex crimes, told the BBC that a "catalogue of disasters" had led to Levy's murders.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme "the patterns were there, he was flying those red flags", and said there were "precursor offences" for which he could have stopped by police."At the moment, the message going out, in my opinion, is that women's safety is not important," she continued.Zoë Billingham, a former independent police inspector who pushed for reforms on how violence against women in girls is policed, said that "too often in cases like this the dots aren't being joined up".She added: "It's not one or two missed opportunities that could have brought him to justice, that could have had him locked up and behind bars and no longer a threat to women and girls. It was an extraordinary succession."

schema.headline: Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'

title: Hunter Biden says pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy
description: Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President J
body: Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy. In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC's Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me.""It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added."It's not fair… All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution - or his father's legacy. He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration."I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted."There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024. Asked about the depths of his addiction, he described drinking almost a gallon of vodka a day while smoking crack cocaine almost every 15 minutes at its worst. "It was hell on earth," he said. "There's nothing glamorous about it."Reflecting on why he turned to drugs and alcohol, Hunter Biden rejected the suggestion that he felt untouchable because he was the son of a president."I wasn't reaching for anything except oblivion," he said. He noted that his addiction was a way to escape feelings of anxiety and isolation. The drugs and alcohol initially felt like a solution before becoming "the thing that almost killed me", he noted. Hunter Biden got emotional at times in the interview, notably when discussing his father's health. Cancer is really hard," he said, stopping to clear his throat. "It's really sad to watch."He revealed that the "cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further. It's very painful" and "very debilitating". "My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family," he said. "He's the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.""The only thing that I say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more."Hunter Biden also reflected on the presidential debate in June 2024 that ultimately ended his father's re-election campaign. He said he had watched it from his home in California and immediately sensed something was wrong."I was shocked," he said. "I knew something was wrong."

schema.headline: Hunter Biden says pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy

title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
description: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on t
body: Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera."I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time."If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman. "Phone photos have warped our perception of time."It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds."Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since. "Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis, external - the inability to choose because there are so many options.When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that"."Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.Additional reporting by Amy Walker.

schema.headline: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'

title: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv
description: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said.In the
body: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, a local official said.In the early hours of Saturday missiles hit east of the capital and witnesses reported hearing powerful explosions just days after strikes across Ukraine killed 21 people.The ballistic missile strikes killed three and wounded another three, head of the regional military administration Timur Tkachenko said, adding that falling debris damaged apartment buildings and cars, while a fire broke out at a separate building.Emergency crews were also fighting fires at a building and fuel tank in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaly Klitchko wrote on Telegram.Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS shared photos showing garages, a business and a building on fire in Kyiv, adding: "The number of victims is being clarified."President Volodymyr Zelensky has arrived in the Serbian capital Belgrade for his first visit. He is meeting with Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić to discuss economic ties, security issues and relations with the European Union.Zelensky is trying to build wider support for Ukraine, but Vučić has refused to apply sanctions to Russia.Serbia is trying to join the EU and has provided aid to Ukraine and promised to help it rebuild after the war.Earlier in the week, Zelensky said delays in receiving anti-ballistic systems from partners leads to "horrific casualties and destruction", saying that having a stronger interceptor capability "could have saved lives" in recent deadly assaults.The president later said the supply of interceptors from allies had been "significantly reduced" this year.It came after Ukraine hit two oil refineries deep inside Russia along with Moscow-linked vessels in the Black Sea, which Zelensky said was intended to limit oil revenues used by Russia to "finance" its war in Ukraine.The Ukrainian military hit Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries during overnight attacks, causing fires at both, the Ukrainian general staff said on Saturday.Recent mediation talks between Ukraine and Russia have faltered, leading to an escalation of attacks between both sides.

schema.headline: Child among three dead in Russian nightly strikes near Kyiv

title: This Olympian curbed his unhealthy porn habit - here are the signs and steps to recovery
description: Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn."Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do
body: Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn."Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset."You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said. So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right. "We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" – like someone might experience with drugs, for example – and how best to deal with it.Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.So what are the markers of an unhealthy porn habit? Neves says it's "not about the frequency or duration, it's about the damage to your life". That might be arriving late to work because you were up all night watching porn, prioritising it above commitments to your loved ones, or watching it in the office, he says.Other crucial questions to ask yourself are whether you can actually cut back or adjust your habit when you try, and whether you carry on watching despite enjoying it less and less, adds Ince, whose research focuses on problematic porn use.For Craig, who describes himself as a recovering addict, it was this loss of control which marked a turning point during the Covid-19 pandemic, when he was in his mid-thirties."I don't think it ever became a huge issue for me until lockdown, where that extra pressure, extra isolation, just compounded the issue."I didn't know how to get it to loosen its grip on me," he recalls.Ince cautions that many people may feel distress about their porn use for social, moral or religious reasons – but that this does not necessarily mean your habit is out of control."Someone could be watching porn for five minutes, three times a week – and because they have a lot of shame, they think 'I'm an addict'," agrees Neves."But then there might be someone who watches it every day and thinks it's fine."Hall similarly encourages clients to "get away from the idea of 'I'm either an addict or I'm not'", and focus instead on how much it is affecting things like your studies and relationships.TV presenter Ore Oduba last year spoke publicly about his 30-year-long porn addiction which began at the age of nine – saying it had been "destroying my life from the inside out"."It was the thing from a very early age that I was running to as a response to a lot of trauma", he told the We Need to Talk podcast last year, before curbing the habit.It is not clear what might cause such behaviour, as experts say much more research is needed."The scientific examination is certainly accelerating, but there is a very long way to go," Ince says.It might begin as something which gives you a break from other issues in your life, says Hall, such as a stressful career or relationship breakdown.There may also be "predisposing factors", such as trauma, issues from early childhood, or negative self-belief, that can make it harder to curb your use, she says.Craig, now 40, says porn became a "tool to turn to for every one of life's ups and downs".He remembers feeling he was "broken, that there was no way out", before recovery helped him to think differently.Hall also points to the impact of the digital environment and people becoming "addicted by design" through algorithms.Both she and Neves say AI-generated porn is making matters worse by enabling people to create "exactly what they want and need", as Neves describes it.If you are worried about your porn use, Ince recommends seeking out support from a qualified and experienced professional.A registered psychologist can be particularly helpful because they may consider your mental health more broadly, "and we know that co-occurring mental health problems are more or less the rule, rather than the exception", he says.This was the case for Craig, who did not realise his porn use may be unhealthy until he started therapy for his mental health."Porn addiction was like a contributing factor," he came to learn.His therapist suggested he join a 12-step programme for sex addiction – a recovery model created by Alcoholics Anonymous – which he credits for his recovery."I didn't necessarily find it easy and straightforward to step away from my addiction. I feel I'm in a good place now, but also acknowledge the fact it's one day at a time."There is currently no central, dedicated NHS service for those struggling with their porn use – although some local services offer support, and you can talk to your GP. This means treatment will more likely come from private practitioners, support groups or online self-help.Ince suggests doing thorough research to find the right fit for you, and cautions against using online resources which may offer generic advice.Some practitioners will help clients towards cutting out porn altogether, while others will help people "integrate it into their lives in a way that is functional," says Neves. Seeking to understand any underlying factors will be a crucial part of treatment, says Hall.There are some practical steps you can take yourself, she says, such as placing blocking software on your device.She also advises recognising when you might feel more susceptible to using porn – which, for some, can be when you are stressed or alone – and planning ahead for what you might do instead.But she says there should ultimately be more support on the NHS, particularly early intervention before porn can take over a person's life.A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: "It is troubling to hear accounts of individuals becoming addicted to pornography at such a young age."It reinforces the importance of the online safety laws we have put in place to prevent children from accessing harmful content."

schema.headline: This Olympian curbed his unhealthy porn habit - here are the signs and steps to recovery

title: Bruno Guimaraes joins Arsenal from Newcastle
description: Arsenal have signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.The former Newcastle captain made it clear he wanted to join the Premier League cha
body: Arsenal have signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.The former Newcastle captain made it clear he wanted to join the Premier League champions earlier this summer. The 28-year-old Brazil midfielder, who has signed a four-year deal with the option of a further 12 months, called the move one of the "toughest decisions" of his life."This move is very tough because Newcastle means so much to me," he added. "But I wanted to experience something new in my life. I feel ready for a new challenge for myself and my family."Newcastle said they wished Guimaraes and his family well.Guimaraes left Newcastle's training camp in La Manga in Spain earlier this week to finalise his move to Emirates Stadium following a breakthrough in talks.He revealed he received messages from a number of his future team-mates, including countryman Gabriel as well as fellow midfielder Declan Rice.Following their previous battles in the middle of the park, Rice told him "come here and please no more fights, now we're friends"."I'm at the point of my life, I think I need a challenge like this," Guimaraes said. "I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I'm in the right place to do it. I'm so excited to start."Guimaraes joined a Newcastle side in relegation trouble in January 2022 and went on to play a crucial role in their improvement in fortunes under former head coach Eddie Howe.The Brazilian became the first captain in seven decades to lift a major domestic trophy for Newcastle after they defeated Liverpool in the 2025 EFL Cup final.He was also part of the side who qualified for the Champions League in 2023 and 2025, before they slipped to 12th place in the Premier League last season.

schema.headline: Bruno Guimaraes joins Arsenal from Newcastle

title: US pledges $1bn support to Colombia as Trump-backed president sworn in
description: The US has pledged £1bn in assistance to Colombia, after the country's new right-wing president was sworn in on Friday.Trump ally Abelardo de la Espri
body: The US has pledged £1bn in assistance to Colombia, after the country's new right-wing president was sworn in on Friday.Trump ally Abelardo de la Espriella used his maiden speech to promise an "all-out war" on what he calls "narco-terrorism".In a statement hailing a "new era in US-Colombia relations", the US state department announced the financial support as part of a "security package" to help de la Espriella achieve "our shared goals", which include fighting organised crime and illegal immigration.The new president's inauguration marks a dramatic shift to the right for Colombia, as he replaces the left-wing former leader Gustavo Petro, who frequently clashed with Trump.Trump endorsed de la Espriella during the election, and said he predicted a "much better relationship" with his new counterpart after his victory in June.A US delegation led by then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has since been confirmed to the post, attended the inauguration. It was also attended by embattled Fifa president Gianni Infantino.De la Espriella chose to take the oath of office not in Colombia's capital, Bogotá, but in the volatile city of Cali, in the west. The change was intended to signal a tough approach to illegal armed groups operating in the region.In his fiery maiden speech - addressing troops at a nearby military base - de la Espriella pledged to crush armed insurgents, rebuild Colombia and defend democracy "by reason or by force".He said "in the age of the Tiger" - his self-appointed nickname - the state would be forceful and decisive against crime."There will not be a single place in our territory where criminals can feel safe," he said.The new president had a successful career as a lawyer representing drug-trafficking paramilitaries, footballers and fraudsters before entering politics. Critics have warned his confrontational style could deepen divisions in an already highly polarised country.De la Espriella has vowed a sharp break with his left-wing predecessor. Instead of holding peace talks with armed groups, he has promised a brutal crackdown on their activities and the construction of mega-prisons.He has also promised a strong military alliance with the US and Israel, in stark contrast to Petro, a long-time critic of Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.In one of his first acts as president, de la Espriella said Colombia would join the "Shield of the Americas" security partnership founded by Trump.The US welcomed this, and said it "stands ready to support the de la Espriella administration's efforts to defeat the vicious narco-terrorist and criminal organisations" that threaten security.The state department also said shared goals included halting illegal immigration through "closer coordination on border security".What Washington calls de la Espriella's "pro-growth agenda" has created an opportunity to "increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries", it added.

schema.headline: US pledges $1bn support to Colombia as Trump-backed president sworn in

title: Scotland closing in on new head coach
description: The Scottish FA is closing in on the appointment of a new head coach to succeed Steve Clarke.Clarke, who had signed a new four-year deal in May, resig
body: The Scottish FA is closing in on the appointment of a new head coach to succeed Steve Clarke.Clarke, who had signed a new four-year deal in May, resigned following Scotland's group-stage exit at the World Cup this summer, ending his seven-year tenure.Scotland return to action in the Nations League with a four-game block of fixtures, which begins away to Slovenia on 26 September.The search for Clarke's replacement is being led by Craig Mulholland, who was appointed as the SFA's chief football officer in May.It is understood Mulholland has spoken to a wide range of candidates from the UK and beyond.Interviews have been conducted and the SFA are nearing an appointment.  It is unclear whether the incoming head coach will be a Scot or foreigner.Steven Naismith, who served as Clarke's assistant, said last month he expects to continue in the national team set-up under a new boss.

schema.headline: Scotland closing in on new head coach

title: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'
description: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegr
body: Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body."Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph."No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school. It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'

title: Carabao Cup: Goals galore - the most astonishing scorelines in competition's history
description: Goals galore - the wildest scores in EFL Cup historyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The EFL Cup has provided some of the highest-scoring game
body: Goals galore - the wildest scores in EFL Cup historyImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The EFL Cup has provided some of the highest-scoring games in English football historyByJude WinterBBC Sport journalistThe Carabao Cup is back.Some clubs use the early rounds to give experience to young players, shake off the last of their pre‑season rust and perhaps sneak an early season upset, but that can also result in some staggering scorelines.From 12‑goal thrillers to 10-0 humiliations and penalty shootouts that threaten to last almost as long as the match itself, the EFL Cup has had it all over the years.Here's a look at the some of the most wild games the competition has ever produced...Dagenham & Redbridge 6–6 Brentford (2-4 pens)Image source, Brentford FCImage caption, The 12-goal thriller between Dagenham and Redbridge and Brentford is the joint-highest scoring tie in EFL Cup historyRound one, 13 August 2014, Victoria RoadLet's start off with a bang and talk about the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history.The tie between Dagenham & Redbridge, then in League Two, and a Brentford side recently promoted to the Championship may not have looked the most interesting on paper, but it certainly delivered a gripping match.A remarkable match was level at 4-4 after 90 minutes and the goals kept coming in extra-time.The Daggers took the lead for the first time in the 113th minute and looked set to progress as they led 6-5 late on, before Brentford's Harlee Dean scored in the 117th minute to take the match to penalties.After Jack Connors and Ashley Chambers missed for Dagenham, skipper Kevin O'Connor stepped up to score the winning spot-kick for Brentford.Wycombe 3-8 Aston VillaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Wycombe threated to shock Aston Villa before the Premier League side scored seven second-half goalsRound two, 20 September 2005, Adams ParkAston Villa manager David O'Leary admitted his side were "on the verge" of being part of a cup shock when they faced Wycombe Wanderers in 2005.But having trailed the League Two side 3-1 at half-time, Villa responded with seven goals in the second half to secure the win.Some Villa fans reacted angrily when goals from Nathan Tyson, Roger Johnson and Tommy Mooney put Wycombe in a strong position at the halfway stage.But goals from Milan Baros and James Milner made it 3-3, before a Craig Easton own goal, two from Gareth Barry and further strikes from Milner and Steven Davis completed an emphatic turnaround.West Ham United 10-0 BuryImage source, West Ham UnitedImage caption, West Ham made it to the fifth round in 1983Second round, second leg, 25 October 1983, Boleyn GroundWe're going back to the days when the early rounds had two legs, the tournament was called the Milk Cup, and the day West Ham United recorded their record win.There was little warning that an eye‑catching scoreline was coming, given John Lyall's Division One leaders had only edged the first‑leg tie 2-1 at Fourth Division Bury.But West Ham raced to a 5-0 half‑time lead, with Alvin Martin, Trevor Brooking and Tony Cottee tearing Bury apart. Cottee completed his hat‑trick before the break and the Hammers were just as ruthless in the second half.Cottee added his fourth, Alan Devonshire got another, Ray Stewart buried a penalty, and Brooking tapped in late on as West Ham reached double figures.Reading 5-7 ArsenalImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arsenal came back from 4-0 down to win 5-7 against ReadingFourth round, 30 October 2012, Madejski StadiumAn incredible match, the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history, and it took extra-time to find a winner.Still without a win in their return to the Premier League, Reading threw away any joy their fans were feeling as they led Arsenal 4-0 by capitulating to lose 7-5.Arsenal found themselves four down after 35 minutes, but Theo Walcott's goal before half‑time sparked a comeback that dragged the match into extra-time. Marouane Chamakh put Arsenal in front for the first time on the night with a goal in the first period of extra-time, only for Reading striker Pavel Pogrebnyak to make it 5-5.But Walcott restored Arsenal's lead before Chamakh completed the scoring.A remarkable night was further added to by the faintly ridiculous moment when Olivier Giroud and Francis Coquelin threw their shirts into the crowd, thinking the match was over, only to have to awkwardly ask for them back once they realised extra‑time was still to come.Manchester City 9-0 Burton AlbionImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester City went on to win the competition in 2019 after sweeping Burton asideSemi-final first leg, 9 January 2019, Etihad StadiumBurton Albion's first major semi‑final was somewhat ruined as they were roundly thrashed by Manchester City.The 3,000 Brewers fans had to battle some M6 chaos just to get there and some might have wished they'd stayed stuck in traffic.Nigel Clough's side had beaten a mixture of Premier League and Championship sides to get to the last four but were powerless to stop a rampant City side.Gabriel Jesus scored four, with Kevin de Bruyne, Oleksandr Zinchenko, Phil Foden, Kyle Walker and Riyad Mahrez also scoring against the beleaguered League One side.After Burton's fairy tale cup run finally ended, Clough said that Pep Guardiola invited him in for a glass of wine and quipped he hoped the Spaniard had "more than a glass."The second leg finished 1-0 at the Pirelli Stadium, sealing a 10–0 aggregate victory for City.Liverpool 10-0 FulhamImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ian Rush (centre) scored twice in Liverpool's double-digit victorySecond round first leg, 23 September 1986, AnfieldLeague champions Liverpool showed their class with a 10-goal demolition of Fulham.Steve McMahon scored four and missed a penalty as the Third Division side were swept aside at Anfield. Ian Rush and John Wark struck early, Ronnie Whelan added a third, and McMahon scored either side of Wark's second. He hit the bar from the spot before making it seven, with further goals from Rush, McMahon and Nicol sealing the club's biggest victory in domestic competition.Liverpool then won the second leg 3-2, advancing 13-2 on aggregate.Preston North End 1-1 Fulham (16-15 pens)Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Preston's penalty shootout win against Fulham is the longest-ever penalty shootout in League Cup historyThird round, 17 September 2024, DeepdaleYes, 1-1 isn't the most memorable scoreline, but the third-round tie between Preston North End and Fulham in 2024 makes it into the record books after producing the longest penalty shootout in the competition's history. A total of 34 spot kicks were taken – 31 of which were successfully converted – as Paul Heckingbottom's men booked their place in round four.Just when it seemed the shootout may never end, Fulham's Timothy Castagne blazed his spot-kick over the bar and Preston midfielder Ryan Ledson – who scored the game's opener in the 36th minute – fired in the decisive penalty.The shootout eclipsed the previous record set in 2016 when Derby County beat Carlisle United 14-13 on penalties.Related topicsFootballEFL CupArsenalReadingLiverpoolFulhamPreston North EndBrentfordAston VillaWycombe WanderersDagenham & RedbridgeBurton Albion

title: Chernobyl evacuee on Welsh family that took him in after disaster
description: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month
body: Chernobyl disaster evacuee 'forever grateful' to Welsh family who took him inImage source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton Honchanka spent a month in Wales as part of the Chernobyl Lifeline programByOscar EdwardsBBC WalesUpdated 2 August 2026In the summer of 1999, 11-year-old Anton Honchanka was looking to escape his contaminated hometown following history's worst nuclear disaster.His journey would take him from Gomel, Belarus, to a United Kingdom that was experiencing a historic total solar eclipse, a major political reshuffle by Prime Minister Tony Blair, and a music chart dominated by singles such as Livin' La Vida Loca.Anton was one of the children evacuated from Belarus following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in neighbouring Ukraine, after a reactor at the plant exploded and spewed out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Due to radiation, parents in Eastern Europe saw the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline program (CCPL) as vital for their children's health with more than 56,000, external coming to the UK for medical aid and humanitarian support.Thirteen years on since the incident, and with the radiation still hanging in the air, Anton had set off on what he saw then as a "new adventure" thanks to the programme, albeit one "not easy" for his mum to see him leave."My mum was really happy that I had the opportunity to go on the trip," said Anton, now 38."But it wasn't easy for her not having me at home."Anton travelled by bus to Minsk, the capital of Belarus, and from there he flew to the UK.His first clear memory upon arriving in the UK was meeting his first host family. "That's where my experience in Wales really began," he said."My first impression was how peaceful and welcoming everything felt. It had such a cosy atmosphere that I felt comfortable almost straight away."Anton said the architecture was "different" from what he was used to in Belarus, with clean streets and a "warm and cosy atmosphere".His trip came at a time when Belarusian people were living in an increasingly authoritarian state, external, according to the UN Refugee Agency, in a period marked by severe political crackdowns and economic stagnation.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton, centre, stood with Dmitry on his left and the Amoss familyAnton and another boy called Dmitry spent the first two weeks with Angela Davies and her sons. Despite the language barrier, he said they all understood each other "perfectly".They were then taken to Llanharry, Rhondda Cynon Taf, to live with Peter and Linda Amoss.They welcomed the boys into their home with "incredible warmth", said Anton, finding ways to "spoil" and "surprise" them."They often took us shopping because they wanted to treat us," he said."They were always thinking about how they could make us smile."Anton said he naturally became great friends with their kids Gethin and Charlotte spending their time playing outside, riding bikes and enjoying their time together."Those are memories I'll always treasure," he added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton visited landmarks such as St Fagans National Museum of HistoryFor Anton, returning home meant going "back to normal life" and he was surprised to find that "nothing had really changed".He and Dmitry gradually lost touch as they lived in different cities."When we arrived in Minsk, I got on a bus to Gomel, and he wasn't on it," he added.Now with two sons of his own, Honchanka said Wales and its people have "stayed in my heart forever"."I would really love to see my host families again if I have the opportunity.""During that time, they became very close and dear to me."Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton said they became his 'second family' during his time in WalesThis year marked 40 years since the Chernobyl nuclear disaster which caused a reactor to start spewing out radioactive material that would spread across swathes of Europe.Children from Belarus and Ukraine stayed with host families for four-week recuperative breaks. The clean air, untainted food and clean water helped to lower the levels of caesium and other radiation stored in the children's bodies.Gerrie Bayley, 74, from Prestatyn, first joined the CPPL in 2004 taking in two girls from Belarus.She enjoyed the experience so much, it has since "become her life" and she now serves as the chair of the charity's north Wales branch.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Dmitry, in the Liverpool shirt, lost contact with Anton when they returned to BelarusGerrie said the few weeks in the UK made a remarkable difference to their health."They would sleep all the time. They had these big black circles under their eyes. "By the end of the month, they had energy and were eating well. I cannot say how much difference it made."The communities rallied around the program providing second-hand clothing, free dentist appointments and eye tests for the children."They all had treatment they needed. So many stores helped out." she said.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton became great friends with the Amoss kids during his stayLinda Amoss, 71, said the family were vetted to make sure they had a spare bedroom with enough capacity to house Anton and Dmitry"As far as they were concerned we were a second family."They had already been in the country for a couple of weeks and we were the second family for the latter two weeks of their stay."Linda said she was told that any time spent outside of Belarus would "benefit their health"."There were children with incredibly high rates of cancer in certain areas," she added.Image source, Anton HonchankaImage caption, Anton has two sons of his own called Dmitry and DemyanLike Anton, she said the language was something they had to overcome, but it ultimately proved no issue as the boys "just clicked in"."Food was sometimes a bit of an issue, but my cooking isn't the best anyway," she added.Anton joined the family on trips to local landmarks such as St Fagans, Oakwood Theme Park and Garth Hill. "I don't remember them being particularly homesick because everything was sort of just so new and bright for them," said Linda.Image source, Linda AmossImage caption, Peter and Linda Amoss looked after Anton for two weeks during his stay As the four weeks drew to a close, Linda said she understood that the chance of the boys being able to return to the UK was "very slim" due to the demand for places in Ukraine and Belarus.Until now, she had not heard from Anton or Dmitry, but said it would be "extremely brilliant" if they could meet in person again.She also takes great pride in Wales' role in the Chernobyl Children's Lifeline programme."Wales is incredibly hospitable, and I really do love that about our country," she added.

title: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information
description: Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financia
body: Richard Tice has said he and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage are suing the National Crime Agency (NCA) over the alleged leaking of confidential financial information.The Boston and Skegness MP and Reform deputy leader told Talk TV they believed the NCA had committed "multiple criminal offences" and said they would be seeking an apology and damages.He accused them of leaking "individual bank statements, bank transfers, details of conversations with bank managers from different banks".Last month Tice wrote to the agency to ask if they would investigate whether they were responsible for the leaking of private financial information to the media.It followed reports that payments made to his company Britain Means Business by the mother of the convicted fraudster George Cottrell were flagged to the NCA as part of its suspicious activity reports (SARs) programme, which alerts law enforcement to potential instances of money laundering.SARs are not crime reports.Tice said at the time he only became aware of it when contacted by the Guardian newspaper, which broke the story.The NCA has been carrying out an internal investigation but Tice told Talk TV it was "playing for time and we've said we're done with it".A Reform UK spokesperson said claims had been filed at the High Court. BBC News has not seen the detail of the claims.A spokesperson for the NCA said: "Following complaints brought by Richard Tice MP and Nigel Farage, the NCA's Professional Standards Unit is conducting an investigation. That work is ongoing. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this time."As first reported by the Telegraph, Tice's company Tisun Investment received a loan of £80,000 from Cottrell in late 2024.That same year, Britain Means Business received a £1m donation from Cottrell's mother.Data from the Electoral Commission shows that Britain Means Business donated £500,000 to Reform UK in the same month.These payments were flagged to the NCA as part of the SARs programme.Cottrell's relationship with Reform has been under scrutiny in recent months after the Sunday Times reported he had supplied Farage with support including security and social media staff in the year before he became an MP.Under parliamentary rules, newly elected MPs have to declare gifts or benefits received in the 12 months before their election that relate to their "parliamentary or political activities".However, there is an exemption for gifts and benefits that are "purely personal".Reform has argued that Farage did not breach the guidelines by not declaring the support from Cottrell because the support was provided in a "purely personal capacity".

schema.headline: Farage and Tice sue NCA over alleged leaks of financial information

title: Todd Blanche, Trump's ex-lawyer, confirmed as attorney general
description: President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche has been confirmed as US attorney general - the nation's top law enforcement official.Bla
body: President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche has been confirmed as US attorney general - the nation's top law enforcement official.Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote, with Republican Senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski opposing him.Senator Bill Cassidy was the deciding vote after announcing he believed Blanche was the best option the president would put forward. Washington had been anxiously waiting for Cassidy's decision, due to years of acrimony between Trump and the senator.The vote brings to an end a lengthy standoff between Senate Republicans and the Trump administration over Blanche, who has served as acting attorney general since April.All Democrats voted against his nomination to lead the Justice Department.Some Republican senators had raised concerns about his handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents and his role in establishing Trump's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund.The fund was planned to provide compensation to individuals who alleged government persecution but critics including Murkowski feared it would go to individuals who were prosecuted for participating in the January 6 attack on Congress.Blanche eventually pledged to walk back the fund after blowback from Republican senators during his confirmation hearings.It remains unclear whether the commitment is legally binding or whether Trump could later persuade Blanche, his former personal attorney, to revive a similar scheme under another name.These issues meant Collins and Murkowski held off on backing Blanche, with the latter citing her lack of confidence in Blanche to "check the worst impulses of this administration".Murkowski announced on Friday she would oppose Blanche, citing concerns over the "politicisation" of the justice department.Collins also raised concerns about Blanche's role in settling Trump's $10 billion lawsuit with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), but said he ultimately trusted Blanche to give the president ​candid legal advice."This is not a referendum on President Trump, it is a decision regarding Mr Blanche, in very specific circumstances," said Cassidy on Friday. "All considered, I will vote for Mr Blanche."Cassidy acknowledged Trump is the ultimate decider on the direction of the justice department, but that Senate confirmation would give Blanche "greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for."Cassidy also said he was reluctant to impede the department's work fighting violent crime.During Trump's second impeachment in 2021, Cassidy voted to convict Trump over the 6 January 2021 Capitol riot. The vote did not pass, and when Trump returned to office, he successfully forced Cassidy into retirement by backing a primary challenger for his Louisiana Senate seat earlier this year.Blanche was already deputy attorney general when he took up the interim leadership role in April, after Pam Bondi was fired.
